subject: Medicine
summary: Chronic pancreatitis is a progressive inflammatory disease of the pancreas that leads to irreversible fibrosis, exocrine and endocrine insufficiency. It is most often caused by alcohol abuse but also by genetic, metabolic, infectious and iatrogenic factors.

sections.p: Chronic pancreatitis is defined by persistent abdominal pain, pancreatic fibrosis on imaging, and evidence of exocrine or endocrine dysfunction. Diagnosis requires at least two of the following: characteristic pain, imaging evidence of fibrosis or ductal changes, and pancreatic function tests showing insufficiency.
b: Pain >3 months, epigastric, radiating to back

t.b: Measures exocrine function; <200 µg/g indicates insufficiency
Normal or mildly elevated; persistently high suggests acute flare
Detects calcifications, ductal strictures, mass effect; confirms fibrosis

sections.p: Severity is staged by the M-ANNHEIM system, which grades pain, exocrine/endocrine insufficiency, imaging findings, and complications. Stages I–IV guide management intensity.
b: Stage I: mild pain, no insufficiency
Stage II: moderate pain, early insufficiency
Stage III: severe pain, significant insufficiency
Stage IV: complications like pseudocyst, ductal obstruction

sections.p: Alcohol abuse is the leading cause worldwide. Other important causes include hereditary mutations (PRSS1, SPINK1, CFTR), autoimmune pancreatitis, metabolic disorders, and infections common in low‑resource settings.
b: Pancreatic duct obstruction by stones or tumors

sections.p: Patients report dull, persistent epigastric pain that may worsen after meals. Weight loss, steatorrhoea, and diabetes are common. Pain may be episodic and can be triggered by alcohol or fatty foods.
Investigations aim to confirm fibrosis, assess function, and rule out mimics. In low‑resource settings, basic labs and ultrasound are useful when advanced imaging is unavailable.

Elevated in autoimmune pancreatitis; supports diagnosis

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening. Red flags include sudden severe pain, jaundice, vomiting, or unexplained weight loss. Complications include pseudocysts, ductal obstruction, diabetes, and pancreatic cancer.
b: Pancreatic cancer – consider in older patients with mass

sections.p: Management focuses on treating the underlying cause, controlling pain, replacing enzymes, and monitoring for complications. Alcohol cessation is paramount. Pain is managed with NSAIDs, opiates, or nerve blocks. Enzyme replacement improves nutrition.
b: Monitor for drug interactions with enzyme therapy

sections.p: Patients require regular follow‑up to assess pain, nutrition, glycaemic control, and imaging. Prevention focuses on alcohol avoidance, early detection of enzyme deficiency, and vaccination against hepatitis.
Chronic pancreatitis can mimic gallstone pancreatitis, peptic ulcer disease, and pancreatic cancer. Distinguishing features include chronic pain pattern, imaging findings, and enzyme levels.
b: Pancreatic cancer – weight loss, mass on imaging

sections.p: Low fecal elastase can be falsely normal in early disease; serum amylase/lipase may remain normal despite fibrosis. Imaging may miss early ductal changes; ultrasound is operator dependent.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain, jaundice, vomiting, unexplained weight loss, new‑onset diabetes, or signs of infection

faq.a: There is no cure; treatment focuses on stopping alcohol, managing pain, replacing enzymes, and monitoring complications.

faq.q: Why do patients develop diabetes in chronic pancreatitis?
faq.a: Fibrosis destroys insulin‑producing islet cells, leading to insulin deficiency.

faq.q: What is the role of enzyme replacement?
faq.a: It restores digestion of fats and proteins, reducing steatorrhoea and improving weight gain.

exam: Explain the diagnostic criteria for chronic pancreatitis and why two of the listed tests are essential.
Describe the M‑ANNHEIM staging system and how it influences management decisions.
Outline the first‑line management for a patient with alcohol‑related chronic pancreatitis presenting with steatorrhoea and mild pain.
